Audi Will Invest $7 Billion in U.S. Plant, While VW Group Shuts Down Plants in Germany
15 photos
Photo: Audi
Audi is considering a massive $3 billion expansion of its upcoming manufacturing plant in the United States, which could bring an additional 3,000 jobs by 2033. That would be on top of the already planned investment of $4 billion that Audi’s CEO announced last month. This is happening while the Volkswagen Group is making efforts to reduce costs by cutting jobs and shutting down plants in Germany.
Just a couple of weeks after the original announcement, Audi is already planning a Phase 2 expansion before it has even broken ground on its facility, set to be built on a 1,500-acre mega-site in Peach County, located just southwest of Macon in Central Georgia.
Audi's CEO Gernot Dollner joined Donald Trump on stage during a political campaign rally held in Perry, Georgia, just a few miles away from the planned site. During the rally, Trump revealed the initial $4 billion investment plan to the crowd before inviting Audi's CEO up on stage to confirm the information and reveal further details.
Gernot Dollner basically looked like the wrong man at the wrong time, because Volkswagen Group is massively investing in U.S. production while executing just as massive a global cost-cutting process to rescue profitability. Besides, he breached compay policy, which bars executives from making public appearances with political candidates or politicians standing for election within three months of a vote.
Photo: Audi That is because fierce competition coming from China, severe overcapacity in Europe, and collapsing profits have driven the auto giant’s profit margins down to an unsustainable 3.8%. To reverse this, the group’s CEO Oliver Blume has secured stakeholder approval for what is turning out to be the largest, most aggressive structural shakeup the firm has been through in its 87-year history.
Cutting jobs in an oversized company Volkswagen employs nearly 630,000 people worldwide, which is significantly more than its main global rival, Toyota. As of the most recent corporate filings from March 31, 2026, Toyota Motor Corporation employs 390,927 people worldwide.
The German group's board officially doubled its restructuring targets, committing to eliminate 100,000 jobs globally by 2030. That is 15% of its entire workforce. In the meantime, the new plant in America will create a total of 7,500 jobs.
Furthermore, Porsche and Audi's European staff are expected to bear a massive portion of these layoffs to protect the group's cash flow. Volkswagen's management has proposed a strict salary freeze until 2030 for roughly 600,000 employees to combat labor costs.
Photo: Volkswagen In the meantime, Volkswagen’s business in China is a full-blown emergency situation, forcing the automaker to completely abandon its decades-long strategy of using the Asian state as an easy profit engine. For nearly 40 years, China generated massive piles of cash that subsidized the rest of Volkswagen’s global operations.
Volkswagen Group's sales strategy in China is cracking However, right now, that system is falling apart, and the group has to rely on its other largest foreign market, North America. And this is exactly what it is doing now, starting with Audi’s footprint in the U.S., which will help the company offset tariffs imposed on imports.
According to documents from the Mid-Georgia Gateway Development Authority, the footprint will scale significantly over the next decade, Automotive News reports . The process will kick off with the already confirmed $4 billion investment. The plant will open in the early 2030s and create 4,500 jobs.
Phase 2 will bring another $3 billion, according to Automotive News. The production hub is expected to be completed by 2033 with a total of 7,500 jobs and an annual output of 200,000 SUVs. Audi will build its largest, heaviest, and most premium flagship SUVs at the new Georgia facility, with the all-new Q9 leading the pack. The Audi Q7 and Q8 will also roll off the production line of the future Georgia plant.
Photo: Audi The Audi Q5 is expected to join them, since it is the undisputed king of sales in America. Audi sold 46,215 Q5s in 2025 and 33,509 units through the first nine months of this year. Its second best-selling model is about halfway there, with 23,581 examples moved in 2025 and 17,866 units sold in 2026.
Georgia is heavily subsidizing Audi's tariff escape Audi is benefiting from massive financial incentives from the state of Georgia, which is thus securing the mega-plant, starting with nearly one billion dollars in total state aid. First, it is offering a 1,500-acre construction site for free, along with $458 million in state tax incentives.
Furthermore, over $120 million will be allocated for the initial construction, rail link improvements, and environmental cleanups, with another $430 million dedicated to local water infrastructure, road upgrades, utility scaling, and workforce recruitment and training.
Audi has been importing 100% of its U.S. inventory from Europe (sedans, e-tron EVs and large SUVs) and Mexico (Audi Q5 with all its variants). Last year, the tariffs imposed by the Trump administration cost Audi a staggering $1.4 billion.
Photo: Audi To bypass this financial bleed, Audi negotiated a deal with federal officials: the U.S. Commerce Department is expected to drop Audi's EU import tariffs from 15% down to about 10% as a direct reward for making this massive domestic manufacturing investment. Audi had initially pushed for a reduction to 7.5%.
The Ingolstadt-based automaker arrives late at the U.S. party. Its main rivals in the segment have been producing vehicles in the United States for decades. BMW opened its giant Spartanburg plant in South Carolina back in 1994. Mercedes-Benz has had its Tuscaloosa, Alabama hub operating since 1996.
